rĕcordātĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
,
a recalling to mind, recollection, remembrance, recordation (class.; esp. freq. in Cic. in sing. and plur.).
With gen.: quorum memoria et recordatio jucunda sane fuit,; so, coupled with memoria,; ; ; cf.: quam (memoriam) quidem Plato recordationem esse vult vitae superioris, (v. recordor init.): veteris memoriae recordatio,the recollection of an old circumstance,; so, praeteritae memoriae,; cf. : habet praeteriti doloris secura recordatio delectationem,; cf. : multorum benefactorum recordatio jucundissima est,: recordatio impudicitiae et stuprorum suorum,; cf.: scelerum suorum, Zumpt and Halm N. cr.: nostrae amicitiae,: suavis,. — With subj.-clause: subiit recordatio egisse me juvenem aeque in quadruplici,.—In the plur.: das mihi jucundas recordationes conscientiae nostrae rerumque earum, quas gessimus,; .—
Absol.: stulti malorum memoriā torquentur, sapientes bona praeterita gratā recordatione renovata delectant, etc.,; cf.: acerba recordatio,: subit recordatio: quot dies quam frigidis rebus absumpsi?.—Plur.: recordationes fugio, quae quasi morte quādam dolorem efficiunt,; .

la:verb:recedo.gloss: to go back, fall back, give ground, retire, withdraw, recede
senses: to go back, fall back, give ground, retire, withdraw, recede
to go away, withdraw, retire, depart from a place; to abandon a thing
la:verb:recedo.html:
rĕ-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3, v. n.,
to go back, fall back, give ground, retire, withdraw, recede.
Lit. (class.; cf.: decedo, abscedo): pone nos recede,: ego abs te procul recedam,: hinc,: illuc,: recedere loco,; cf.: centuriones ex eo quo stabant loco recesserunt,: non modo illum e Galliā non discessisse, sed ne a Mutinā quidem recessisse,: procul a telo veniente,: de medio,: ab hoste,: longius,: tristis recedo,; : ab Illiturgi,: in castra Corneliana, —
In partic., to retire to one's bedchamber, go to rest, ; .—
Transf.
Of inanimate and abstract things: ut illae undae ad alios accedant, ab aliis autem recedant,: verba movere loco, quamvis invita recedant,yield,: multa ferunt anni venientes commoda secum, Multa recedentes adimunt,the departing years,: abeant ac recedant voces illae,.—
Of places, things, etc., to stand back, recede (i. e. to be distant or retired; freq., esp. after the Aug. per.): secreta parentis Anchisae domus arboribusque obtecta recessit,; cf. ; and: etsi lata recessit Urbe domus,; : Palaestina vocabatur, quā contingit Arabas ... et quā recedit intus, Damascena,: Magna Graecia in tres sinus recedens Ausonii maris,; ; .—Of nations: gens Cappadocum longissime Ponticarum omnium introrsus recedens,.—In a painting, etc.: pictor vi artis suae efficit, ut quaedam eminere in opere, quaedam recessisse credamus,; cf.: venter recessit,.—Poet., of places, which appear to recede by our departure from them: provehimur portu, terraeque urbesque recedunt,: mea terra recedit,; ; ; —
In gen., to go away, withdraw, retire, depart from a place, to abandon a thing, = discedere.
Lit. (in good prose very rare), = discedere, haec effatu' pater, germana, repente recessit, vanished, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 48 Vahl.): nec vero a stabulis pluviā impendente recedunt Longius (apes),; .—
Transf., of things, to separate from any thing (with which it was previously connected): in aliis ossibus ex toto saepe fragmentum a fragmento recedit,: carnes ab ossibus,; : caput e cervice,; for which also: caput cervice,; cf. ; . —
Trop., to withdraw, depart, desist (class.; esp. freq. in Cic. and Quint.): si quid vos per laborem recte feceritis, labor ille a vobis cito recedet, Cato ap. : avius a verā longe ratione recedit,: senes, ut in otia tuta recedant, aiunt, etc.,: ab officio recedere,; ; : ab armis,i. e. to lay them down,: penitus a naturā,: ab eodem exemplo,; ; : a sententiis ejus, ab omni voluntate, consiliisque,: a vitā, i. e. to kill one's self, (but , to die, in gen., a doubtful conjecture; Jahn, procedente

vitā): a veritatis viā longe,: ab oppugnatione,.—Very freq. of inanimate and abstract subjects: postquam recessit vita patrio corpore,: (nomen hostis) a peregrino recessit et proprie in eo, qui arma contra ferret, remansit,has lost the signification of foreigner,; so, res a consuetudine,; : figurae sententiarum ab illo simplici modo indicandi recedunt,: ab usu cotidiano, et saep.—Poet., with simple abl.: sic nunquam corde recedit Nata tuo,departs,.—Absol., to vanish, pass away, disappear: et pariter Phoebes, pariter maris ira recessit,: spes,: quonam nostri tibi cura recessit?: fortuna recessit,.— With in: in ventos vita recessit,passed away into the winds,.— Hence, * rĕcessus, a, um, P. a. (acc. to I. B.), drawn back, receding: scaena recessior,standing farther back,.

la:verb:recipio.gloss: to take back, (i.e., regain possession of something)
senses: to take back, (i.e., regain possession of something)
to take upon oneself, undertake, accept (esp. when done as a duty or under an obligation. Cf. suscipiō)
la:verb:recipio.html:
rĕ-cĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3 (
fut. apoc. recipie, for recipiam, Cato ap. and 236 Müll.; v. dico init.: recepso, for recepero,), v. a.
capio
.
To take back, get back, bring back; to retake, regain, recover.
Lit. (very freq. and class.): dandis recipiendisque meritis,: tu me sequere ad trapezitam . . . recipe actutum, (just before, ni argentum refers); cf.: centum talenta et credidisse eos constat, et non recepisse,; and (opp. mutuum dare) : si velit suos recipere, obsides sibi remittat,: obsides,: reges,: recepto amico,; . — Freq. of places, etc., once captured and lost, to retake: cum Tarento amisso ... aliquot post annos Maximus id oppidum recepisset ... nunquam ego (Tarentum) recepissem, nisi tu perdidisses,; cf. : Lavinium,; so of other things: recipere suas res amissas,: praeda omnis recepta est,: signa, quae ademerant Parthi,: arma,; : pectore in adverso totum cui comminus ensem Condidit assurgenti, et multā morte recepit, drew out again, = retraxit, ; so, sagittam ab alterā parte,: suos omnes incolumes receperunt (sc. ex oppido in castra), drew off, withdrew, = reduxerunt, ; so, milites defessos,: exercitum,: equitatum navibus ad se intra munitiones,: illum ego ... medio ex hoste recepi,bore away, rescued,.—
With se, to draw back, withdraw from or to any place, to betake one's self anywhere; in milit. lang., to retire, retreat: se ex eo loco,; cf.: se e fano,: se ex opere,: se ex hisce locis,: se e Siciliā,: se ex fugā,; : se inde,: se hinc, et saep.: recipe te,: se, (just before, reverti); (coupled with loco excedere); 3, 46; cf.: sui recipiendi facultas,; ; for which: se recipiendi spatium,: recipe te ad erum,: se ad dominum,: se ad nos,: se ad suos,; ; ; ; fin.: se ad Caesarem (Allobroges, legati),; : se ad agmen,; : se penitus ad extremos fines,: se ad legionem,fin.: se ad oppidum llerdam,: se ad ordines suos,: se ad signa,; : se a pabulo ad stabulum,: inde se in currus,: se ex castris in oppidum,: se in castra,. 11 fin.; 2, 24; 3, 6; 3, 26 fin.; 4, 15 et saep.: se in fines,: se in Galliam,fin.: se in montem,: se in antiquas munitiones, : se in silvas ad suos,: se in castra ad urbem,; ; cf.: se retro in castra,; and with this cf.: sese retro in Bruttios,; and so, se, with rursus,; ; ; ; et saep.: se in novissimos,: se intra munitiones,; cf.: se intra montes,: se per declive,: se sub murum,: se trans Rhenum,: se Larissam versus,: se domum ex hostibus,: se domum,; ; : se Adrumetum,: se Hispalim,: se Dyrrhachium ad Pompeium,fin.: se illuc,; ; ; cf.: se huc esum ad praesepim suam,: se eo, et saep. — In the same meaning, without se: neque sepulcrum, quo recipiat, habeat portum corporis, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 415 Vahl.); cf. of a military retreat: si quo erat longius prodeundum aut celerius recipiendum,; so without se after the verbum finitum several times in Plaut.: rursum in portum recipimus,: dum recipis,: actutum face recipias,. —
Transf.
In business lang., to keep back, retain, reserve (cf. ): posticulum hoc recepit, quom aedis vendidit,; so in a sale, Crassus ap. ; ; ; : mulier magnam dotem dat et magnam pecuniam recipit, Cato ap. . — With object-clause, . — With dat.: aqua, itinere, actu domini usioni recipitur,.—
To restore (late Lat.): urbem munitissimam,to fortify anew,. —
Trop., to get back, bring back; to receive again, regain, recover: ut antiquam frequentiam recipere vastam ac desertam bellis urbem paterentur,: jus,: et totidem, quot dixit, verba recepit,got back,: quam (vitam) postquam recepi,received again,: anhelitum, to recover one's breath, ; ; cf. spiritum,: animam,; , prooem. § 13;: a tanto pavore recipere animos, Weissenb.: a pavore animum,: e pavore recepto animo,; for which: animos ex pavore,: recepto animo,; : animum vultumque,: mente receptā,: (vocem) ab acutissimo sono usque ad gravissimum sonum recipere,to bring it back,. — In zeugma (cf. I. A. supra): arma et animos,.—
With se.
To betake one's self, withdraw, retire from or to any place: ad ingenium vetus versutum te recipis tuum,: ad frugem bonam,: ad reliquam cogitationem belli,: se a voluptatibus in otium,: se in principem,to resume his princely air,.— More freq.,
To recover, to collect one's self: difficulter se recipiunt,regain strength,: quae cum intuerer stupens, ut me recepi, Quis hic, inquam, etc.,: nullum spatium respirandi recipiendique se dedit,: se ex terrore ac fugā,: se ex timore,: se ex fugā,: nondum totā me mente recepi,.
(Acc. to re, I. b.) To take to one's self, admit, accept, receive; constr. with the simple acc., with ad, or in and acc., in and abl., with simple abl., with a local acc.
Lit.
With simple acc.: quos homines quondam Laurentis terra recepit, Enn. ap. Prisc. p 762 P. (Ann. v. 35 Vahl.): (ego) excludor, ille recipitur,: aliquem,: hic nulla munitio est, quae perterritos recipiat,; cf.: hos tutissimus portus recipiebat,; ; cf. fin.; 3, 35: eum Jugurtha accuratissime recepit,: neque quisquam aut expulsus invidiosius aut receptus est laetius,; ; : nisi nos vicina Trivici Villa recepisset,

et saep.: quisnam istic fluvius est, quem non recipiat mare?; cf. ; and: (Peneus) accipit amnem Orcon nec recipit,i. e. does not take it to itself, does not mingle with it,: equus frenum recepit,received, submitted to,: necesse erat, ab latere aperto tela recipi,. —

With ad: recipe me ad te,; ; ; ; ; : aliquem ad epulas,; cf.: ad lusum,. —
With in and acc.: recipe me in tectum,: concubinam in aedes,: nos in custodiam tuam,: Tarquinium in civitatem,; ; ; : aliquem in ordinem senatorium,: aliquem in fidem,; ; ; : aliquem in civitatem,: aliquem in caelum,: aliquem in deditionem,; ; : aliquem in jus dicionemque,: aliquem in amicitiam,; Kritz N. cr.: aliquam in matrimonium,; et saep. —
With in and abl. (rare and in purely local relations; v. Kritz ad ): aliquem in loco,: loricati in equis recipiuntur, Auct. B. Hisp. 4, 2: sidera in caelo recepta, (but in , the correct read. is tuto Hexapylo, without in; v. Weissenb. ad h. l.). — (ε) With simple abl. (mostly in purely local relations): ut tuo recipias tecto servesque nos,; so, aliquem tecto,: exercitum tectis ac sedibus suis,: aliquem suis urbibus,: aliquem civitate,: aliquem finibus suis,; fin.: aliquem oppido ac portu,; fin.: aliquem moenibus,: Romulus caelo receptus,: receptus Terra Neptunus, et saep. — (ζ) With local acc.: me Acheruntem recipere Orcus noluit,: aliquem domum suam,; cf.: aliquem domum ad se hospitio,.— (η) Absol.: plerosque hi, qui receperant, celant,.—
Transf.
In business lang., to take in, receive as the proceeds of any thing: dena milia sestertia ex melle,: pecuniam ex novis vectigalibus,: pecunia, quae recipi potest,. —
In gladiator's lang.: recipe ferrum, receive your death-blow, the cry of the people to a vanquished gladiator whom they were not inclined to spare, ; Kühn.; ; for which: totum telum corpore,; and: ense recepto, Corte.—
Milit. t. t., to seize, capture, take possession of, occupy: mittit in Siciliam Curionem pro praetore cum legionibus duo; eundem, cum Siciliam recepisset, etc.,: Praeneste non vi, sed per deditionem receptum est,: Aegyptum sine certamine,: eo oppido recepto,: civitatem,; 7, 90; ; ; ; 3, 16: Aetoliam,: rempublicam armis,: Alciden terra recepta vocat,the subjugated earth,. —
In the later medical lang., of medicines, to receive, i. e. be compounded of various ingredients: antidotos recipit haec: stoechados, marrubii, etc.,; so ; 28; 37; 52 al. (hence the mod. Lat. receptum, receipt, and recipe).—
Trop.
To take to or upon one's self, to assume; to receive, accept, admit, allow, ἐνδέχομαι: non edepol istaec tua dicta nunc in aures recipio,; cf. : jusjurandum,; ; cf. : in semet ipsum religionem recipere, to draw upon one's self, : quae legibus cauta sunt, quae persuasione in mores recepta sunt,admitted,; cf. : antiquitas recepit fabulas . . . haec aetas autem respuit,; cf. : nec inconstantiam virtus recipit nec varietatem natura patitur,; cf. : non recipit istam Conjunctionem honestas, 3, 33, 119: assentatio nocere nemini potest, nisi ei, qui eam recipit atque eă delectatur,: timor misericordiam non recipit,: casus recipere (res),to admit, be liable to,; so, aliquem casum (res),: re jam non ultra recipiente cunctationem,; : sed hoc distinctionem recipit, pr.: si recipiatur poëtica fabulositas,: in hoc genere prorsus recipio hanc brevem annotationem,; cf. : nos necessarios maxime atque in usum receptos (tropos) exequemur,; cf. ; ; ; so with a subj.-clause, ; ; —
Of opinions, etc., to adopt, embrace (late Lat.): alicujus sententiam,: opinionem,.—
In partic.
To take upon one's self, undertake, accept the performance of a task consigned or intrusted to one (whereas suscipio denotes, in gen., the voluntary undertaking of any action; cf.: spondeo, stipulor, polliceor): recepi causam Siciliae ... ego tamen hoc onere suscepto et receptā causā Siciliensi amplexus animo sum aliquanto amplius. Suscepi enim causam totius ordinis, etc.,: in hoc judicio mihi Siculorum causam receptam, populi Romani susceptam esse videor,; and: in quo est illa magna offensio vel neglegentiae susceptis rebus vel perfidiae receptis,; cf. also : verebamini, ne non id facerem, quod recepissem semel?: causam Sex. Roscii,: mandatum,: officium,: curam ad se,.—
To take an obligation upon one's self, to pledge one's self, pass one's word, be surety for a thing, to warrant, promise, engage a thing to any one, = ἀναδέχομαι (a favorite word of Cic., esp. in his Epistles): Pe. Tute unus si recipere hoc ad te dicis ... Pa. Dico et recipio Ad me, ; cf.: ad me recipio: Faciet,: promitto in meque recipio, fore eum, etc.,; cf.: spondeo in meque recipio eos esse, etc.,.—With obj.-clause: promitto, recipio, spondeo, C. Caesarem talem semper fore civem, qualis hodie sit,; so with hoc, (with spondeo); 6, 12, 3; 13, 41, 2 (with confirmo); ; Caecin. ap. ; Drak.; 33, 13 fin.: pro Cassio et te, si quid me velitis recipere, recipiam,. — With de: de aestate polliceris vel potius recipis,; ; cf. also: sed fidem recepisse sibi et ipsum et Appium de me,had given him a solemn assurance,.— With dat. (after the analogy of promitto, polliceor, spondeo): ea, quae tibi promitto ac recipio,; cf.: omnia ei et petenti recepi et ultro pollicitus sum, Planc. ap. ; : mihi,; : quid sibi is de me recepisset, in memoriam redegit,.—With dat. and obj.-clause: mihi in Cumano diligentissime se, ut annui essemus, defensurum receperat,; so, Manut. (with confirmare); 13, 72, 1; Planc. ap. ; ; —
In jurid. lang.: recipere nomen, of the prætor, to receive or entertain a charge against one, ; ; Cael. ap. ; ; for which: recipere reum,; : aliquem inter reos,; 13, 10. —Hence,
rĕceptus, a, um, P. a. (acc. to II. B. 1.), received, usual, current, customary (post-class. and very rare): auctoritas receptior,: scriptores receptissimi, Sol. praef.—
rĕceptum, i, n.subst. (acc. to II. B. 2. b.), an engagement, obligation, guaranty: satis est factum Siculis, satis promisso nostro ac recepto,; cf.: promissum et receptum intervertit,.

la:verb:recreo.gloss: to create again or anew, restore, recreate
senses: to create again or anew, restore, recreate
la:verb:recreo.html:
rĕ-crĕo, āvi, ātum, v. a.,
to make or create anew, to remake, reproduce, restore, renew (very rare; syn.: reficio, reparo): lumen,; ; cf. : carnes,. — Poet.: Athenae recreaverunt vitam legesque rogarunt, transformed, reformed life (by agriculture), ; ; ; cf., of baptism,; and, jocosely: illic homo homines non alit, verum educat Recreatque, he does not merely feed men, but fattens and transforms them (by much eating), . —
In gen., to restore to a good condition, to revive, refresh, recruit, invigorate in body or mind; and, mid., to become refreshed or recruited, to recover, revive (freq. and class.; syn.: reficio, relevo, erigo, confirmo).
In body: propterea capitur cibus, ut suffulciat artus Et recreet vires interdatus, ; cf. : voculam,: ex vulnere,; : ex gravi morbo,: aspectu smaragdi recreatur acies,: lassitudines,; cf. defectionem,: leni vento umerum,: arbor aestivā recreatur aurā,: tenuatum corpus,: potorem squillis,: semivivum ex acie elatum,: fessos maniplos,.—
In mind: quae (litterae) mihi quiddam quasi animulae restillarunt: recreatum enim me non queo dicere,revivified,: reficere et recreare mentem,; so coupled with reficere,; cf.: (discipulus) mutatione recreabitur sicut in cibis, quorum diversitate reficitur stomachus,: afflictum erexit, perditumque recreavit,restored again to life,; cf.: provinciam afflictam, et perditam erigere atque recreare,: ego recreavi afflictos animos bonorum,: res publica revirescat et recreetur,: non recreatus neque restitutus populus,: recreatur civitas,: (animus) cum se collegit atque recreavit,has recovered itself,: litteris sustentor et recreor,: Caesarem Pierio recreatis antro,: spatium interponendum ad recreandos animos, * et saep.: se ex magno timore,: recreatus ex metu mortis,: ab hoc maerore recreari,: se ab illo tumore, Auct. B. Alex. 37 fin.: veritas debilitata tandem aequitate talium virorum recreëtur,.—With gen.: recreatur animi,; , p. 168, 21.

senses: to fall back, return (especially of an evil)
la:verb:recido.html:
rĕ-cīdo, di, sum, 3, v. a.
caedo

to cut away, cut down, cut off (mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose).
Lit.: vepres,; cf.: malleolos ad imum articulum,: sceptrum imo de stirpe,; for which: laurum imā stirpe, (cf. II.): ceras inanes,empty cells,: hirsutam barbam falce,: caput,: immedicabile vulnus Ense recidendum est,: pollicem alicui,: comas,; cf. capillos,: ungues,: columnas,to hew out,: fustes,: ancile ab omni parte recisum,: mella,i. e. to take out,.— Of persons: cuncti simul ense recisi,cut down,.— Poet.: fulgorem sideribus,to rob the stars of their brightness,: gramina morsu,to devour,.—

la:noun:recessus.gloss: a going back, receding, retiring, retreat, departure
senses: a going back, receding, retiring, retreat, departure
la:noun:recessus.html:
rĕcessus, ūs, m.
recedo
,
a going back, receding, retiring, retreat, departure; opp. accessus (class.; cf. receptus): accessus ad res salutares, a pestiferis recessus,: ut luna accessu et recessu suo lumen accipiat,.— Of the ebb of the tide: quid de fretis aut de marinis aestibus plura dicam? quorum accessus et recessus lunae motu gubernantur,; so : recessum primis ultimi non dabant, i. e. means of retreat, * ; Cael. ap. : gemmae,its removal from the eye,: cum processui et recessui cani juberet, i. e. in going home, Treb. Gall. 17, 3; .—
Meton. (abstr. pro concreto), a distant, retired, or secret spot, a nook, corner, retreat, recess (acc. to recedo, I. B. 2.; syn.: secessus, secretum): mihi solitudo et recessus provincia est,; cf.: nos terrarum ac libertatis extremos recessus ipse ac sinus famae in hunc diem defendit,our remote position itself and our distant renown,: nec, sicut aestivas aves, statim auctumno tecta ac recessum circumspicere,: cum vox quasi in recessu oris auditur,: hic spelunca fuit, vasto submota recessu,in a deep recess,; cf. ; ; : ubi marmoreo Superi sedere recessu,in the marble hall,: oculi in recessu cavo,.—In plur., ; (along with anguli); ; ; ; ; ; ; .—
Trop.: tum accessus a te ad causam facti, tum recessus,advances and retreats,: habeat illa in dicendo admiratio ac summa laus umbram aliquam et recessum, quo magis id, quod erit illuminatum, extare atque eminere videatur,somewhat of shade and background,; cf.: haec professio plus habet in recessu quam fronte promittit,.—In plur.: vita hominum altos recessus magnasque latebras habet,: in animis hominum tantae latebrae sunt et tanti recessus,: strenua ingenia, quo plus recessus sumunt,leisure,.

, that has not long existed, fresh, young, recent (opp. vetus, and differing from novus; v. antiquus init. With ad and acc.: recentes sumus ad id quod incipimus,.—

B. Afr. 78, 6. — Hence, advv.: recens and recenter, lately, freshly, newly, just, recently, etc.

Form rĕcen-ter (post-class.): capti turdi,: lecta poma,—
Sup.: quam recentissime stercorato solo,; so, res gestae,.

la:verb:recordor.gloss: to call to mind, remember, recall, recollect
senses: to call to mind, remember, recall, recollect
la:verb:recordor.html:
rĕ-cordor, ātus, 1,
v. dep. a. and n.
cor
.
To think over, bethink one's self of, be mindful of a thing (as the result of the reminisci, the recalling of it to memory), to call to mind, remember, recollect (freq. and class.; cf. recognosco): quod jam pueri ita celeriter res innumerabiles arripiant, ut eas non tum primum arripere videantur, sed reminisci et recordari. Haec sunt Platonis fere,; cf. : sed parum est me hoc meminisse: spero etiam te, qui oblivisci nihil soles, nisi injurias, reminiscentem recordari,.— Constr.
With acc. (so most freq.): pueritiae memoriam,: omnes gradus aetatis tuae (with considero),: desperationes eorum,: hujus meritum in me, Wund. N. cr.: tua consilia,: δέρρεις, : excusationem legationis obeundae,: communes belli casus,: virtutes (Manlii),: acta pueritiae,: priorem libertatem,: feralem introitum,: bene facta priora,: vocem Anchisae magni voltumque,: antiqua damna, et saep.: tuam virtutem animique magnitudinem,; so, tua in me studia et officia multum tecum,; cf.: alicujus vitam et naturam,; : si rite audita recordor,: cum recorder non M. Brutum ... sed legiones nostras in eum locum saepe profectas,.— With quod: recordatus quod nihil cuiquam toto die praestitisset,: ad ea, quae ... recordanda et cogitanda,.—
With obj.-clause: recordabantur, eadem se superiore anno in Hispaniā perpessos, Caes. B. C. 3, 47; : hoc genus poenae saepe in improbos civis esse usurpatum recordatur. ; ; and, acc. to the analogy of memini, with inf. pres.: ego recordor longe omnibus unum anteferre Demosthenem,.—
With rel.-clause: admonitus re ipsā recordor, quantum hae quaestiones punctorum nobis detraxerint,; : recordor unde ceciderim,; ; .—
With gen. (freq. in late Lat.; in Cic. only in two foll. passages, for in , the true read. is meritum): recordans superioris tuae transmissionis,: flagitiorum suorum recordabitur,: pacti mei,: nominis Domini, id. Amos, 6, 11: verborum, et saep.—(ε) With de: tu si meliore memoriā es, velim scire, ecquid de te recordere,; ; ; ; .— (ζ) Absol.: et, ut recordor, tibi meam (epistulam) misi,.—
To think of, meditate, ponder something future (rare): nunc ego non tantum, quae sum passura, recordor,: omnium captivitatem et miserrimam servitutem,.?*!
Act. collat. form recordavit, Quadrig. ap. ; .—
Part. perf. in a pass. signif.: ad recordata poenalis vitae debita,preserved in the memory,

la:verb:recurro.html:
rĕ-curro, curri (recucurrit, only ), 3, v. n.,
to run back, hasten back (class.).
Lit.: ego ad anum recurro rursum,; cf.: recurrit rursus ad Hispalim Caesar, Auct. B. Hisp. 40 fin.: ad me,; ; cf. : ad raedam,: in Tusculanum,: in arcem,: rure,: recipe te et recurre,: jam huc recurret,: luna tum crescendo, tum defectionibus in initia recurrendo,; cf. : ad fontem Xanthi versa recurret aqua,; cf.: in suos fontes versa aqua,.—Poet., of the revolving of the sun, * ; and of the year,.—With a homogeneous object: coeptum saepe recurrat iter,. —
Trop.
In gen., to come back, turn back, return, revert, recur: cur posteris amplior honor quam majoribus haberetur? curve non retro quoque recurreret aequitas eadem?; cf. : naturam expellas furca, tamen usque recurret,: mox Bruma recurrit iners,; cf.: recurrat versa hiems,: valetudines anniversariae ac tempore certo recurrentes,: ad easdem conditiones,; cf.: uti eo recurrant,: cum ea unde generata, quo recurrant, viderit,whither they return,; . — With dat.: haec appellatio memoriae recurret,will recur to memory, (with admoneri and recordari): recurrentes versus = reciproci,; . —
In partic., pregn., to have recourse to, to resort, recur to any thing (very rare; usu. decurro, q. v.): ad eam rationem recurrunt, ut, etc.,; so, ad eos auctores, etc., id. prooem. § 17.

la:verb:recuso.html:
rĕ-cūso, āvi, ātum, 1 (
gen. plur. of the part. pres. recusantūm, ), v. a.
causa
.
In gen., to make an objection against, in statement or reply; to decline, reject, refuse, be reluctant or unwilling to do a thing, etc. (freq. and class.; cf.: abnuo, renuo, denego); constr. with acc., an inf., an object-clause, with de, ne, quin, quominus, or absol.
With acc.: uxorem, * ; : me judicem,; cf.: populum Romanum disceptatorem,: populi Romani amicitiam,: nec quae pepigere recusent,: nullum periculum communis salutis causā,; so, nullum periculum,; : laborem,fin.; ; : nihil nisi hiberna,: legumina,: servitutem,: vincla (leones),: jussa, et saep.: nihil tibi a me postulanti recusabo,; so, psalteria virginibus probis,: nihil de poenā,; cf.: de stipendio,: qui quod ab altero postularent, in se recusarent,: Ptolemaeus recusabat regem Aridaeum,rejected,. — Of things: terra numquam recusat imperium,: genua impediunt cursumque recusant,: rapax ignis non umquam alimenta recusat,: (falsae gemmae) recusant limae probationem, et saep. —
With inf. (in class. prose, only in negative sentences or questions implying a negative): mori recusare,; Planc. ap. ; ; Anton. ap. ; : hoc facere,: ad minora se demittere, Quint. prooem. § 5: prodere voce suā quemquam aut opponere morti,: praeceptis parere,: quicquam tentare,: tibi comes ire,. 704: facere ipse,; Plin.

Pan. 5; ; .— Of things: pedes vitiosum ferre recusant Corpus,; so ; .—

With object-clause: non rem (medicam) antiqui damnabant, sed artem. Maxime vero quaestum esse manipretio vitae recusabant,: Velinum lacum obstrui recusantes,refusing to permit,; cf. infra, II.—
With de: de judiciis transferendis recusare,.—(ε) With ne: Servilius et recusare et deprecari, ne iniquis judicibus ... judicium capitis in se constitueretur,: sententiam ne diceret, recusavit,: reliqui ... ne unus omnes antecederet, recusarent,— (ζ) With quin: si absim, haud recusem, quin mihi male sit,: non possumus, quin alii a nobis dissentiant, recusare,: non recuso quin, etc.,; ; : neque recusare ... quin armis contendant,; .— (η) With quominus: nec recusabo, quominus omnes mea legant,; : ... quominus perpetuo sub illorum dicione essent,: neque recusavit quo minus poenam subiret,.—(θ) Absol.: non recuso, non abnuo, etc.,: recusandi aut deprecandi causā legatos mittere,; et saep. —
In partic.
To refute, disprove: nativitatis mendacium,.—
In jurid. lang., to protest against a complaint; to object, take exception, plead in defence: causa omnis, in quā pars altera agentis est, altera recusantis,: numquid recusas contra me?: tu me ad verbum vocas: non ante venio, quam recusaro ... Quoniam satis recusavi, veniam jam quo vocas,: cum reus recusare vellet, sub usuris creditam esse pecuniam, etc.,; cf. recusatio, II. B.

la:noun:receptus.html:
rĕceptus, ūs, m.
recipio
.
A drawing back (very rare).
Lit.: spiritus ... in receptu difficilis,hard to recover,. —
Trop., a retraction, recantation: receptus nimis pertinacis sententiae,. —
Milit. t. t., a drawing or falling back, a retiring, retreat (very freq. in prose and poetry): ut expeditum ad suos receptum habeant,; so, habere receptum ad aliquem,; and simply receptus habere,; Planc. ap. ; ; : cum receptus primis non esset,; : dare receptum alicui,; fin.; and simply receptus dare,fin.: Caesar receptui cani jussit,; cf.: receptui signum audire,: signum dare receptui,: Caesar receptui suorum timens,; : receptui sibi consulebant,, § 4: haud facili inde receptu,: ne receptum amittam, Pompon. ap. , C, 2 et saep.: canere receptui a miseriis contemplandis, to give the signal for leaving off, etc., . — In plur.: (bucina) cecinit jussos inflata receptus,: cane, Musa, receptus,leave off,; and in the signif., place of retreat, refuge: tuti recessus,: perdices surculis receptus suos vestiunt,nests, (cf. receptaculum, II. fin.).—
Transf., a going back, retreating: receptus et recursus maris,i. e. the ebb and flow,—
Trop., a retiring, falling back, retreat: receptui canente receptu,; cf. : receptus ad Caesaris gratiam atque amicitiam,: receptum ad poenitendum habere,: ad expertam clementiam,: a malis consiliis receptum,; . 23, 2.

la:verb:recito.html:
rĕ-cĭto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
In the best prose, a publicist's t. t., to read out, recite a document, statement, report, etc., in public proceedings: alicujus testimonium,; cf.: testimonia tabulasve,: litteras in concione,: litteras in senatu,; ; ; cf. ; ; : edictum,; : orationem,: nolo cetera recitare,: epistulam meam,: quid ego nunc hic Chlori testimonium recitem?: rogationem suam populo,: testamentum,: recitet ex codice,; so, responsum ex scripto,: de tabulis publicis,: auctionem populi Romani de legis scripto,: elogium de testamento,.— Of persons: testamento si recitatus heres esset pupillus Cornelius,; so, heres,: aliquem praeterire in recitando senatu,in the list of senators,; so, senatum,: aut recitatis in actione, aut nominatis testibus, by reading over the witnesses (i. e. their testimony) or by simply naming them, ; v. Spald. ad h. l. —
In gen., to read out, recite any thing in public (freq. since the Aug. per., after which it became customary to recite one's own works before audiences; cf.: pronuntio, declamo): To. At clare recitato. Do. Tace, dum perlego, : postquam recitasti quod erat cerae creditum,: in medio, qui Scripta foro recitent, sunt multi,; cf. ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; 2, 10, 6 et saep. al.—With dat.: nec recitem cuiquam nisi amicis,: Quinctilio si quid recitares,: nec illi ... verba ultra suppeditavere quam ut sacramentum recitaret,.—
To repeat from memory, say by heart, recite: quin etiam recitare, si qua meminerunt, cogendi sunt (phrenetici),; . —
Of prayers, to say, offer (eccl. Lat.): orationes,.

la:verb:recognosco.html:
rĕ-cognosco, gnōvi, gnĭtum, 3, v. a.
To know again, recollect, recall to mind, recognize, i. q. recordor (class.; esp. freq. in Cic.): se non tum illa discere, sed reminiscendo recognoscere, (just before, recordari); cf. : fugam et furtum,, § 18: ea, quae scit, mecum recognoscere,; cf. : noctem illam superiorem mecum recognosce,; : cum te penitus recognovi, timere desino,; cf.: personas quasdam,: in quibus (litteris) mirificum tuum erga me amorem recognovi, Cass. ap. ; so, res (suas),: spatia certaminum,: dona templorum,: cuncta loca,: sacra eruta annalibus,; cf.: ille se imperatorem cognosceret,feel himself,. —
To look over, review, investigate, examine, inspect, i. q. recenseo (so most freq. since the Aug. per.): quoniam non recognoscimus nunc leges populi Romani sed aut repetimus ereptas aut novas scribimus,: socios navales,; cf. : peregrinos,: equitum turmas,; ; ; : agros,: ergastula,

In partic., to examine a writing in respect to its genuineness and value; to certify, authenticate: tabulas in foro summā hominum frequentiā exscribo ... Haec omnia summā curā et diligentiā recognita et collata et ab hominibus honestissimis obsignata sunt,; cf.: decretum Pompeii,: codicem,: descriptum et recognitum,; ; : libellos recognoscere et emendare,to revise and correct,.

capio
,
to get or obtain again; to regain, recover, etc. (good prose; cf.: reparo, redimo).

Trop.
To obtain again, regain, recover: si et vos et me ipsum reciperaro,; cf.: illum per te,: adulescentulos,to gain over again, regain,: se quiete reciperare,to recruit, recover themselves,; so mid.: radices arborum reciperantur,.—
To revive, restore (late Lat.): crede Deo et reciperabit te,: templum,.

la:verb:reconcilio.html:
rĕ-concĭlĭo, āvi, ātum, 1 (old

Caesare reducit, reconciliat, restituit in gratiam,: inimicos in gratiam,; cf.: quibus eum omnibus eadem res publica reconciliavit, quae alienarat,reunited, reconciled,: aliquem alicui,; ; ; ; ; cf.: animum sorori tuae,: militum animos imperatori,: voluntatem senatus nobis,: mundum deo,: aliquem, to make friendly, conciliate, Caes. ap. , C, 1: cura reconciliandi eos in gratiam,: inimicos,; .—To recover, regain: oratione Parum insulam,; to re-establish, restore: quod scribis de reconciliatā nostrā, gratiā, non intellego, cur reconciliatam esse dicas, quae nunquam imminuta est,restored,: gratiam,; 3, 12, 4; ; : existimationem judiciorum amissam,: diuturni laboris detrimentum sollertiā et virtute militum brevi reconciliatur,: gratiam cum aliquo,; fin.; cf.: gratiam cum Thebanis,; : concordiam,; : amicitiam de integro,; for which: inimicitiam invicem,i. e. to appease, (corresp. to the previous inimicos): voluntatem, Planc. ap. : pacem,; ; ; .—Absol., .—

rĕ-crūdesco, dŭi, 3,
v. inch. n., to become raw again. *

la:verb:recludo.html:
rē^-clūdo (-claudo, Coripp. 3 Joann. 118), si, sum, 3, v. a.

Pan. 5; ; .— Of things: pedes vitiosum ferre recusant Corpus,; so ; .—
